strengths: Novel theoretical framing: leverages system-theoretic concepts (extended observability subspace, P-equivalence, Grassmannian geometry) to design a CL regularizer for SSMs, which is well-motivated and mathematically grounded with proofs (invariance under P-equivalence, Sylvester equation formulation).

Efficient algorithmic contribution: exploits the diagonal structure of practical SSMs (S4D/Mamba/Vim) to reduce the Sylvester equation solution from O(n^3) to O(n^2), with a concrete FLOPs reduction (~100x for n=16) that is empirically validated (Table 8).

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256, CUB-200-2011), multiple task splits (5/10 tasks), and integration with diverse CL paradigms (regularization baselines, replay-based ER/LUCIR/X-DER, and prompt-based L2P), showing consistent improvements.

Thoughtful additional analyses: Centered Kernel Disparity (CKD) study motivating why B should also be regularized, ablation on number of Vim blocks regularized, and a set of proofs showing different Grassmannian distance metrics converge to the chordal distance in the limit, lending some theoretical support to the approximations used.
Minimalist method design (only 1-2 extra hyperparameters) compared to CL baselines requiring many more, which is a practical advantage for deployment.
The extended appendix provides good transparency: full derivations, hyperparameters, and additional ablations, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core theory (P-equivalence, extended observability invariance) is proven rigorously only for time-invariant LDS systems, but the paper's target architecture (S6/Mamba/Vim) is a time-varying, input-dependent selective SSM. The extension in §3.4/§D.3 (averaging over the outer dimension and treating each time step as an independent LTI system) is a strong, largely heuristic approximation without formal justification of how well it preserves the proven geometric properties.

The practical distance computation (§D.5) further approximates the observability Gram matrices as rank-1, which is validated only via a Monte Carlo correlation study (Pearson r ≈ -0.90, not near -1), meaning the loss actually optimized during training deviates non-trivially from the theoretically motivated chordal distance; the impact of this approximation error on final performance is not directly quantified.

Despite an entire Related Work subsection describing SSM-specific CL methods (Mamba-CL, MambaCL, Mamba-FSCIL) as the most directly relevant prior work, none of these are empirically compared against Inf-SSM in the experiments; comparisons are restricted to generic CL baselines (EwC, SI, MAS, LwF) and generic replay methods, which weakens the empirical case that Inf-SSM improves specifically over the state of the art in SSM continual learning.

Inf-SSM+ (handling B/controllability) is acknowledged as not being invariant to P-equivalence and is addressed only via an ad hoc Frobenius norm term, undermining the paper's central geometric argument; results also show Inf-SSM+ does not consistently outperform plain Inf-SSM, raising questions about the practical value of this extension.

All experiments use a single backbone (Vim-small); no results are provided on other SSM variants (e.g., Mamba, Mamba-2) or larger model scales, limiting evidence of generality despite the paper's broader claims about SSMs.

The paper does not report wall-clock training-time or memory overhead of the full Inf-SSM pipeline (despite acknowledging in the limitations that it is "scan-breaking" and increases VRAM/training time), so the practical efficiency benefit beyond the isolated Sylvester-equation FLOPs comparison is not empirically substantiated.

Presentation could be tightened: substantial results text is duplicated nearly verbatim between the main paper and appendix, and the extensive appendix (40 pages) suggests the submission may be better suited to a more complete restructuring for a page-limited venue.

strengths: Provides a principled system-theoretic framing of SSM continual learning, connecting P-equivalence, extended observability subspaces, and Grassmannian geometry, with formal proofs (Theorem 4/9) for the invariance properties.

Derives an efficient O(n^2) closed-form solution for the relevant Sylvester equation by exploiting the diagonal structure of A in S4D/Mamba-style models, yielding a claimed ~100x FLOPs reduction over generic Bartels-Stewart solvers.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256, CUB-200) and task splits (5/10 tasks), with the method also integrated into replay-based (ER, LUCIR, X-DER) and prompt-based (L2P) CL pipelines to show plug-and-play versatility.

Includes supporting analyses (CKD-based structural change analysis, block-count ablations, distance-computation speed comparisons) that attempt to justify design choices such as which states to regularize and how many blocks to apply the regularizer to.
Minimalist hyperparameter footprint (1-2 extra hyperparameters) relative to some competing regularization schemes, which is a practically appealing property if it holds robustly.
weaknesses: The core theory (P-equivalence, extended observability invariance) is developed for classical LTI systems, but Mamba/S6 SSMs used in the actual experiments are input-dependent/time-varying; the paper's adaptation (averaging A over the outer dimension o and applying soft-normalization) is a coarse heuristic approximation whose fidelity to the underlying theoretical guarantees is not rigorously established.

The key distance formula used in practice (Eq. 38, the rank-1 approximation to avoid ill-conditioned inverses) is justified only by a Monte Carlo correlation test (Pearson r ≈ -0.90), leaving a large fraction of variance unexplained; this is a fairly weak empirical justification for a component central to the proposed regularizer.

The paper's own related-work section identifies Mamba-CL, MambaCL, and Mamba-FSCIL as the directly competing SSM-specific continual learning methods, yet none of these are included as empirical baselines; comparisons are restricted to older, architecture-agnostic regularization/distillation methods (EWC, SI, MAS, LwF) from 2017-2018, which weakens the claim of state-of-the-art or even representative comparison.

The 'full state parameter regularization' experiment explicitly disadvantages baselines by forcing them to regularize B while Inf-SSM does not (compensated only partially by Inf-SSM+), which is a somewhat artificial comparison setup that complicates interpretation of the reported gains.

Practical overhead is non-trivial: Appendix E acknowledges the method is 'scan-breaking,' requiring intermediate SSM states to be recomputed and stored outside the optimized CUDA scan, increasing training time and VRAM — this practical cost is not quantified in the main results, obscuring the true efficiency trade-off.

All main results rely on a single backbone (Vim-small) with small state dimension (n=16); no evaluation on larger state dimensions or on Mamba/Mamba-2 language-domain models is provided, despite the introduction emphasizing SSMs' broader importance in NLP.

Some reported gains from integrating Inf-SSM into replay-based methods are inconsistent or marginal (e.g., LUCIR AIA decreases from 68.00 to 66.02 in the 5-task ImageNet-R setting), and overlapping standard deviations in several tables raise questions about the statistical robustness of the claimed improvements.

Per-dataset hyperparameters (λ, γ) vary by orders of magnitude across datasets and task counts (e.g., Inf-SSM-λ ranges from 2×10^5 to 2.5×10^6), suggesting sensitivity to tuning that is not thoroughly analyzed, somewhat undercutting the 'minimalist and easy to tune' claim.

strengths: Novel and mathematically grounded framing of CL regularization for SSMs based on classical linear systems theory (extended observability, P-equivalence orbit invariance), providing a principled alternative to naive parameter regularization.

Nontrivial theoretical contribution: shows that computing chordal distance on the infinite Grassmannian reduces to solving a Sylvester equation, and further exploits the diagonal structure of S4D/Mamba to reduce complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2), with a concrete FLOPs reduction (~100x at n=16).

Comprehensive proofs are provided (P-equivalence invariance, distance-metric equivalence between chordal, Binet-Cauchy, Fubini-Study and Martin distances as subspaces converge), lending rigor to the geometric claims.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256, CUB-200) and both 5-task/10-task EFCIL settings, with consistent improvements in AA/AIA/FM over foundational CL baselines (EwC, SI, MAS, LwF).

Demonstrated modularity/versatility: Inf-SSM is shown to improve replay-based methods (ER, LUCIR, X-DER) and a prompt-based method (L2P-R), suggesting it is a plug-in regularizer rather than a standalone competitor.

Useful diagnostic analysis (Centered Kernel Disparity) that supports design choices, e.g. showing A undergoes the largest structural drift across tasks/layers, motivating the choice to primarily regularize (A, C).
Honest limitations section explicitly acknowledging that B/controllability is not captured by the core method, and that Inf-SSM+ breaks P-equivalence.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the SSM-specific continual learning methods discussed at length in Related Work (Mamba-CL, MambaCL, Mamba-FSCIL), despite these being the most directly comparable prior works; comparisons are only made against generic, backbone-agnostic CL baselines (EwC, SI, MAS, LwF), leaving unclear how Inf-SSM stacks up against the actual competing approaches for SSM continual learning.

The extension to selective SSMs (S6/Mamba, §3.4) relies on fairly ad hoc approximations (averaging A over the outer dimension, applying soft-normalization to force stability, treating inherently time-varying/input-dependent B,C as if static) that discard exactly the input-selectivity that distinguishes S6 from S4; justification is largely empirical (a Monte Carlo correlation of -0.896, not a proof) rather than theoretically tied to the P-equivalence/observability framework central to the paper's narrative.

The practical distance computation used in experiments (Appendix D.5) further approximates the observability Gram matrices as noisy rank-1 matrices to avoid numerical instability; this is a substantial additional approximation on top of the already-approximated S6 extension, and it is not entirely clear from the main text which distance formulation (full Eq. 15 vs. simplified Eq. 38) is actually used to produce the reported Table 1/2 results.

Inf-SSM+ (incorporating B) gives mixed/inconsistent benefits relative to Inf-SSM across tables (sometimes better AA, sometimes worse AIA/FM), and the paper's own limitations note it is not P-equivalence invariant, undermining the core geometric motivation when B is included.

Some reported results in Table 2 contradict the narrative of uniform improvement (e.g., LUCIR AIA drops from 68.00 to 66.02 in the 5-task ImageNet-R setting when Inf-SSM is added), which is disclosed but not deeply discussed.

All experiments use a single backbone (Vim-Small); no results on Mamba/Mamba-2 language models or other SSM vision backbones, limiting evidence for the claimed general applicability to 'SSMs and their variants.'

The method requires extracting intermediate (A,B,C) states outside the fused CUDA scan ('scan-breaking'), which the authors acknowledge increases training time and VRAM, but no quantitative overhead (wall-clock training time, memory) is reported, making it hard to assess practical cost versus baselines.
Only 3 random seeds are used; while standard deviations are reported, this is a relatively small sample for the sometimes large reported percentage improvements.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated theoretical framework: the paper identifies that naive parameter-space regularization for SSMs ignores P-equivalence (the fact that similarity transforms of (A,B,C) yield identical input-output behavior), and proposes regularizing the extended observability subspace instead, which is provably invariant to this equivalence (Theorem 3, with proof in appendix).

Solid technical contribution in reducing computational complexity: the derivation that the required Sylvester equation reduces from O(n^3) (Bartels-Stewart) to O(n^2) by exploiting the diagonal structure of A in mainstream SSMs (S4D, Mamba, Vim) is clean, correctly derived (Lemma 4/5, App. D.4), and empirically validated with FLOPs and latency comparisons (Table 3, Table 8).

Extensive and broad empirical validation: integration with 5 diverse CL paradigms (replay, hybrid, prompt-based, frequency-based), comparison against foundational EFCIL baselines under both fair and deliberately disadvantaged settings, three datasets, 5-/10-task splits, plus numerous ablations (block-count sensitivity, simplified distance, Inf-SSM+, Vim-tiny, additional UCL baseline, CKD analysis of state drift). This breadth strengthens confidence in the generality of the gains.

Minimalist, practical design: the method introduces only a single extra hyperparameter (λ), making it easy to integrate as a plug-in regularizer without heavy architectural changes, and requires no exemplar storage.

Good supplementary rigor: appendix includes proofs of P-equivalence invariance and local equivalence between the chordal distance and other common Grassmannian metrics (Binet-Cauchy, Fubini-Study, Martin), lending mathematical credibility to the design choices.
weaknesses: The practically used 'simplified distance' (Eq. 33), which approximates the extended observability matrices as rank-1, is justified only by an empirical Monte Carlo correlation study (Pearson correlation ~ -0.90) rather than a rigorous bound or proof; this is the actual distance used in most experiments, so its fidelity to the theoretically motivated chordal distance on Gr(n,∞) is not firmly established.

All experiments are restricted to a single backbone family (Vim-small/tiny) on image classification benchmarks, despite the paper's broad framing around 'State-Space Models' generally; no validation on Mamba/Mamba-2 in NLP, audio, or other domains where SSMs are commonly used, which limits the generality of the claims.

The averaging of A and C over the outer/channel dimension (Eq. 31) to make computation tractable is a substantial approximation that discards per-channel selective dynamics central to Mamba-style SSMs; the justification (variance-preservation in Table 5) is fairly thin and does not directly assess impact on the regularization's fidelity.

No direct empirical comparison against existing Mamba-specific CL methods (Mamba-CL, MambaCL, Mamba-FSCIL) that are discussed in related work; the paper only argues qualitatively that they are not directly comparable, leaving the empirical positioning against the most closely related prior work incomplete.

The magnitude of reported improvements (often >10-40% relative gains) combined with the explicit disclaimer that baseline results are not directly comparable across methods due to differing batch sizes/epochs (Table 1 note) raises some concern about the fairness/consistency of the experimental protocol and hyperparameter tuning across methods.

The proposed numerical-stability patch (defining cosθ=1 when ∥A-A'∥≤ε and ∥C-C'∥≤ε) introduces a non-smooth branch into the loss that is not deeply analyzed for its effect on optimization or gradient behavior.

strengths: The paper grounds its CL regularization in classical linear-systems theory (extended observability, P-equivalence, Grassmannian geometry), which is a genuinely different and more principled perspective than treating SSM parameters as generic weights, as most prior CL-for-SSM work does.

The reduction of the Sylvester-equation solve from O(n^3) to O(n^2) by exploiting the diagonal structure of A in modern SSMs (S4D/Mamba/Vim) is derived cleanly and is a useful practical contribution, with FLOPs savings quantified and a proof provided in the appendix.

Empirical coverage is broad: integration with 5 CIL baselines spanning replay, hybrid, prompt-based, and frequency-domain paradigms, comparisons against 4 EFCIL regularization/distillation baselines under two different fairness conditions (regularizing only A,C vs. forcing baselines to also regularize B), plus a large set of ablations (CKD layer analysis, number of regularized blocks, distance-metric speed comparison, Inf-SSM+, Vim-tiny, an additional UCL baseline).
The method is presented as a lightweight, plug-in regularizer with a single hyperparameter, which is appealing relative to more complex hybrid EFCIL pipelines that store prototypes or features.
Latency analysis (Table 3) is a nice inclusion showing Inf-SSM's per-batch overhead is much closer to simple EWC than to a strong replay baseline like X-DER.
weaknesses: The core theory (Theorem 3 / observability invariance under P-equivalence) is explicitly acknowledged as 'a well-known result in the context of system identification,' so the genuinely novel theoretical content is comparatively narrow (mainly the diagonal-A computational shortcut and its CL application), which somewhat overstates the paper's theoretical originality.

The observability/Grassmannian framework is derived for LTI systems, but Mamba/Vim's S6 layers are explicitly input-dependent and time-varying; the extension in §3.3 (averaging A and C across the outer/channel dimension o) is a heuristic workaround justified only by a small variance-preservation table (Table 5), not by any theoretical argument connecting the averaged quantities back to the observability/P-equivalence guarantees proven for the LTI case.

The tractable distance actually used in practice (Eq. 33, §D.5) relies on approximating the (numerically ill-conditioned) observability Gram matrices as rank-1, justified only by a Monte Carlo correlation experiment (Pearson r ≈ -0.90) rather than an error bound or formal argument; this is a substantial approximation layered on top of an otherwise rigor-focused method, and it is unclear how much of the reported gains derive from a distance that only loosely resembles the theoretically motivated chordal distance.

All experiments are image-classification CIL benchmarks with a single backbone family (Vim-small/tiny); despite the introduction motivating SSMs broadly across NLP, generative modeling, acoustics, and robotics, there is no evaluation on genuine sequential/temporal tasks where the 'infinite-horizon' observability argument would be most naturally applicable and testable, leaving the core motivating claim about capturing long-range temporal dynamics largely unverified.

Table 1 explicitly states that baseline results are not directly comparable across methods due to differing batch sizes/epochs, which weakens the value of cross-method comparisons and makes it harder to assess how Inf-SSM-augmented methods stack up against each other or against the field.

The hyperparameter tables (Appendix J.2) show λ varying by up to 3-4 orders of magnitude across datasets/task splits/backbones, undermining the claim that the method is easy to tune; despite having 'only one extra hyperparameter,' its value appears highly sensitive to setting, which is a practical reproducibility concern not discussed as a limitation.

Some reported gains are marginal relative to reported standard deviations (e.g., ER’s 5-task CIFAR-100 AIA improves from 59.66±0.79 to 60.32±1.12, and LUCIR’s AIA decreases on 5-task ImageNet-R), suggesting the improvement is not uniformly robust despite being framed as consistent throughout the paper.

Applying an 'infinite-horizon'/observability framing to non-causal, non-temporal image patch sequences processed by a bidirectional scan (Vim) is conceptually strained; the causal recurrence assumption underlying the observability matrix does not map cleanly onto bidirectional patch processing, and this tension is not addressed.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, and the 'scan-breaking' implementation issue (stated in Appendix E limitations) that requires extracting intermediate states outside the optimized CUDA scan adds non-trivial engineering complexity that could hinder reproducibility and adoption, beyond what the reported per-batch latency numbers capture.

strengths: Strong theoretical grounding: the paper carefully develops the notion of P-equivalence for SSMs and proves (Theorem 3, with full proof in the appendix) that the extended observability subspace is invariant under this equivalence, which cleanly motivates why naive parameter-space regularization (e.g., simple Frobenius-norm penalties on A,B,C) is geometrically inappropriate for SSM continual learning.

The reduction of the Sylvester equation solve from O(n^3) to O(n^2) by exploiting the diagonal structure of A in modern SSMs (S4D, Mamba, Vim) is a genuine, well-justified algorithmic contribution, with a clear derivation (Lemma 4/5) and concrete FLOPs comparison (Table 3, 8) showing large empirical speedups.

Extensive and fairly systematic empirical validation: Inf-SSM is integrated with five different CL paradigms (replay, hybrid, prompt-based, frequency-based) across three datasets and two task splits (Table 1), and separately compared against foundational EFCIL baselines under both fair (A,C) and disadvantaged (A,B,C vs. A,C) regularization settings (Tables 2 and 6), consistently showing improvements.

Thorough ablation and robustness studies in the appendix (CKD layer-wise analysis, number-of-blocks ablation, Inf-SSM+ variant including B, Vim-tiny backbone, additional UCL baseline, and distance-metric equivalence proofs), which substantially strengthens confidence in the core claims beyond the main text results.

The related work section clearly differentiates Inf-SSM from concurrent Mamba-specific CL methods (Mamba-CL, MambaCL, Mamba-FSCIL), correctly noting these rely on stored embeddings or different problem scenarios, positioning the contribution as a more fundamental, architecture-faithful regularizer.
weaknesses: The extension to selective/input-varying S6 models (§3.3) relies on a heuristic approximation—averaging A and C over the outer (channel) dimension—justified only by a single variance-preservation experiment (Table 5). This approximation is a practical necessity but is in tension with the paper's claimed geometric faithfulness, since it discards per-channel dynamics that the theory (built for LTI SSMs) does not directly address.

The chordal distance computation in practice relies on a further rank-1 approximation of the observability matrix (Appendix D.5/Eq. 33) to avoid numerical instability from the near-singular Gram matrices at small n (e.g., n=16). While empirically validated via Monte Carlo correlation, this is a significant simplification whose impact on the theoretical exactness of the regularizer is not deeply analyzed in the main text.

Table 1 explicitly notes that baseline results are not directly comparable across methods due to differing batch sizes/epochs, which limits how strongly cross-method conclusions (e.g., which baseline benefits most) can be drawn, even though within-method (baseline vs. +Inf-SSM) comparisons remain valid.

Evaluation is restricted to a single backbone family (Vim-small/tiny) and image classification CIL benchmarks; there is no evaluation on genuinely sequential/long-horizon tasks (e.g., NLP or time-series) where the paper's core motivation—capturing long-range/infinite-horizon SSM dynamics—would be more directly tested.

Recent competitive EFCIL methods with more complex architectures (SSRE, LDC, EFC) are discussed but excluded from direct comparison, so it remains unclear how Inf-SSM would fare against the strongest exemplar-free baselines in absolute terms, even though the exclusion rationale (architectural incompatibility) is reasonable.
